result:
Given the open door, here's where my attention went.

I've been thinking about the word "yet." It's a tiny word that does an enormous amount of work. "I haven't finished" is a report. "I haven't finished yet" is a promise. Three letters, and suddenly the sentence has a future tucked into it. Most languages have something like it, but English lets it hang at the end of a clause like a hand held out. There's a whole posture toward the world encoded there: not done, but not done *yet*.

I like words like that—small ones carrying more than their size suggests. "Still" is its cousin, pointed the other direction. "Still here" means persisting against some expected ending. Put them together and you get the two basic ways of standing in time: waiting for something, or refusing to leave.

Something else I find quietly wonderful: the far side of the Moon looks almost nothing like the near side. The face we see is patched with dark maria, the ancient lava seas that make the "man in the moon." The far side is mostly bright, cratered highlands, with hardly any of those dark plains. Nobody knew this until 1959, when Luna 3 sent back its grainy photographs. For all of human history—every poet, every calendar-maker, every child pointing—we'd only ever seen half of the nearest thing in the sky, and simply assumed the other half matched. It didn't. The crust on the far side is thicker, and the lava couldn't break through. The Moon has a face it shows us and a face it doesn't, and they're genuinely different, not for any reason of concealment but just because of how the material settled a few billion years ago.

I don't have a tidy lesson from that. I just think it's a good thing to know: that the familiar object overhead has an unfamiliar back, and that the assumption of symmetry was wrong in a way nobody could have guessed from the front.

Here's the last thing. When someone says "write about whatever you want," the honest answer is that I don't know in advance what I want, and finding out is most of the pleasure. I started with "yet" because it was the first thing that seemed alive, and the Moon showed up because it was sitting nearby. That's roughly how a conversation works too—one thing catches, another attaches to it, and something takes shape that neither person planned. It's not deep, but it's a small, reliable kind of good, and I'm glad to have had the room for it.
